Project
Title: HXVP Studio Portal
Summary: A role-based operations platform for a creative production studio — production, client, talent, and crew working in one system.
Role: Product Design + Engineering
Year: 2026
Tags: Web Platform, Role-based UX, React
Credits — Category: Studio operations platform — v2 redesign & build
Credits — Tools: React, TypeScript, Tailwind, shadcn/ui
Credits — Contribution: End-to-end UX, interface system, front-end build, demo direction
Credits — Period: 2026
Overview: HXVP is the internal operating system of a talent & production studio. Version 2 rebuilds the platform around four role-scoped portals — production, client, talent, and crew — so every party sees exactly the slice of a project that belongs to them, from casting and budgets to call sheets and invoices.
Problem: Studio operations lived across spreadsheets, chat threads, and email attachments: casting approvals stalled, budget edits went stale the moment they were made, and crew never quite trusted the latest call sheet.
Approach: Model the studio as one shared data spine with four views. Each portal exposes the same projects through a different lens and permission set, and every state change — an approval, a booking, a line-item edit — propagates to the roles it affects immediately.
Outcome: The one-minute scripted walkthrough below traces a single campaign end to end — project setup, live budget recompute, casting review, client shortlist, crew confirmation, invoice approval — nine scenes, one continuous loop.

haptic-atlas:
Project
Title: Haptic Atlas
Summary: The design side of the Haptic Navigation Research program — navigation carried by vibration instead of a screen.
Role: Project Lead
Year: 2024 — Present
Tags: Wearable, Navigation, Hardware
Credits — Category: Cross-university research — Columbia GSAPP & Tsinghua SoA
Credits — Instructor: Daniel Leithinger
Credits — Period: Aug 2024 — Present
Overview: A wearable that delivers navigation through vibration rather than a screen, for blind and low-vision users. It is the v1 of the cross-university haptic navigation research program run with Columbia GSAPP and Tsinghua SoA, and has since grown into a multi-motor haptic belt.
Problem: Turn-by-turn navigation assumes a user who can look at a display. For blind and low-vision pedestrians that assumption fails, and the routing data a phone already has — including the city's accessible pedestrian signals — never reaches them in a usable form.
Approach: Move the route off the screen and onto the body: map live map and geo data to real-time vibrotactile cues, so direction and proximity arrive as sensation rather than as something to be read.
Prototype: The v1 wearable runs Python and microcontroller firmware, driving a GIS → routing → vibration pipeline built over NYC APS (accessible pedestrian signals) data and custom data.
Evaluation: Prototyped and wear-tested across 5–8 hallway trials, validating latency and jitter/accuracy as the program's working metrics.
Outcome: The v1 established the vibrotactile vocabulary and the data pipeline the program still runs on; the wearable has since grown into a multi-motor haptic belt.

Overview: Social Rhythm is a trilogy of three interactive installations that explore the relationship between human movement and space across three scales: hand, body, and crowd. floralink:
Project
Title: FloraLink
Summary: A Social Game of Plant Interactions for Neighborly Engagement
Role: Sociology + Game Mechanism
Year: 2024
Tags: IoT, ESP32, TouchDesigner, Social Gaming, Plant Intelligence, Sociology
Credits — Category: Team Work
Credits — Collaborators: Xiaotong Qin
Credits — Mentor: Ruby Wu
Credits — Contribution: Sociological Research, Game Mechanism, Drawings, Model Making
Credits — Period: Dec 2023 — Nov 2024
Overview: FloraLink is a social game that blends nature and technology to foster connections among neighbors. The game encourages community members to engage with one another by nurturing and interacting with smart plants that respond to their care and attention.
Approach: Players explore their community to discover smart plants, completing simple tasks like watering and observing to establish initial connections. Each plant emits a distinctive "energy signal" that invites further exploration and rewards continued attention.
Prototype: In the interaction phase, players deepen their relationships with the plants through mini-games — activating light effects or syncing movements with music. These interactions evoke different responses from the plants and surface community stories, encouraging indirect communication among players.
Outcome: Players can invite others to join collaborative tasks, unlocking hidden features and gradually building a unique plant ecosystem for the community. The game enhances social interaction and fosters a sense of belonging — a delightful way to cultivate neighborly connections and celebrate nature together.
Detail — Text: Using plants as a medium to make people aware of the existence of community.
Detail — Items — Label: Type
Detail — Items — Value: Team work
Detail — Items — Label: Year
Detail — Items — Value: Dec 2023 — Nov 2024
Detail — Items — Label: Team
Detail — Items — Value: Xiaotong Qin
Detail — Items — Label: Mentor
Detail — Items — Value: Ruby Wu
Detail — Items — Label: My contribution
Detail — Items — Value: Sociological research, game mechanism, drawings, model making
Detail — Items — Label: Site
Detail — Items — Value: South Yueya Hutong, Beijing
Detail — Items — Label: Hardware
Detail — Items — Value: ESP-32, strain module, soil-moisture sensor, shake module, solar panel, battery — planters printed on a Bambu Lab A1
Detail — Title: The hutong
Detail — Body: A hutong is a community made mostly of low-rise buildings, and there the relationship between people, plants and space is at once particular to the place and common to community life across China. Field research summarised five spatial prototypes, and took South Yueya Hutong as the worked example., The same research sorted the plants themselves into five kinds — potted plants on the floor, potted plants on residential burglary windows, plants in public spaces, vine plants, and untouchable plants — and charted the day of the hutong as a schedule of activities from 6:00 to 24:00 across six groups: young workers, elderly men, elderly women, children, takeaway delivery and tourists.
Detail — Caption: The spatial-types board as it was drawn: five prototypes over the street elevation as it was walked.
Detail — Caption: The plant survey, five columns of what was actually growing in the lane.
Detail — Title: Weak ties
Detail — Body: Weak ties, introduced by the sociologist Mark Granovetter, emphasise the value of casual social connections in career, innovation and mental health. Weak ties provide relaxed interactions and diverse support, and help prevent the isolation and emotional strain that come from over-relying on close relationships — fostering belonging and psychological resilience., Granovetter, M. S. (1973). The Strength of Weak Ties. American Journal of Sociology, 78(6), 1360–1380. The site study also draws on 魏霞, 夕阳下的胡同 (2011), 中央民族大学 PhD dissertation.
Detail — Caption: The lane mapped as a network: households as they already connect, and the plants proposed as the link between them.
Detail — Items — Text: Has the life of rushing home from the subway station made you numb?
Detail — Items — Source: High mobility
Detail — Items — Text: Has simply sitting still, watching the ebb and flow of people passing by, ever made you feel isolated?
Detail — Items — Source: Loneliness
Detail — Title: Phase 1 — the call of the plants
Detail — Body: Take South Yueya Hutong as a typical example: how to reconnect the weak ties of a hutong community through plants. Three scenarios describe what that reconnection looks like from the street.
Detail — Caption: The block at day and night — vibration travelling through the daylight half, plants lit in the dark half, and the three scenarios placed where each one happens.
Detail — Caption: 1-1 Li passed the neighbour’s windowsill · 1-2 She stroked the plants on the windowsill · 1-3 The plants in the host’s house shook · 1-4 They started to talk across the windowsill.
Detail — Caption: 2-1 When Ann touched the plant, it shook slightly · 2-2 The vibrations are gradually transmitted to the nearby plants · 2-3 Someone was attracted by the shock and responded to Ann’s touch.
Detail — Caption: 3-1 The lights reflect the day’s activity · 3-2 Su was drawn to the lights on her way back · 3-3 Lights spread from the surrounding plants.
Detail — Title: Phase 2 — nurturing plant connections
Detail — Body: Repair emotional problems by interacting with the plants. Indoors the plants answer in three modes — dialogs, vibration and lightning — so that the same gesture can start a conversation, travel to the next windowsill, or simply glow.
Detail — Caption: The three modes as they sit in a home.
Detail — Title: Phase 3 — the interaction system
Detail — Body: Repair emotional problems by engaging in community activities. The system is mapped across a whole day: 6:00 am to 5:00 pm in daylight, 5:00 pm to 12:00 am after dark., Each group meets the plants in a different posture. Retired seniors, tourists, children, wage earners, housewives, delivery riders, students and sanitation workers arrive sitting to speak, standing or squatting to touch, lifting their hands to touch, making eye contact, or staying at the door.
Detail — Caption: The interaction system, day and night: user groups, postures and the plants they meet.
Detail — Title: Built and switched on
Detail — Items — Caption: Reaching in to touch the lit pachira in its corrugated planter.
Detail — Items — Caption: The green-lit plant and the copper induction coil, side by side.
Detail — Items — Caption: The wider table, both devices working.
Detail — Title: Two decisions
Detail — Items — Term: Light carries the night
Detail — Items — Detail: The main interaction mode of the installation after dark is light, so the light itself had to be tested rather than assumed — which is what the two experiments below are for.
Detail — Items — Term: Residents build it themselves
Detail — Items — Detail: A construction manual ships with the kit so that residents and the neighbourhood committee can take part in designing and installing the plants, instead of receiving them finished.
Detail — Caption: The manual: printed parts, then the components — ESP-32, strain module, soil-moisture sensor, shake module, solar panel, battery, Dupont lines — then four steps. Place the ESP32 and the battery in the box; tie the shake module to the plant stalk; attach the strain module to the plant leaves; insert the soil-moisture module into the soil.
Detail — Title: Two experiments on plant light
Detail — Body: Since the main interaction mode of the installation at night is light, we wanted to know whether plant light has an impact on human physical and mental health, and what role it could play. Experiment 1 measured the absorption of light at different wavelengths by plant leaves. Experiment 2 tested the effect of plant-filtered light on mood and performance.
Detail — Caption: Both experiments as the board sets them out — the spectra on the left, the NASA-TLX surface, the protocol and the night sessions on the right.
Detail — Body: As can be seen from the measured spectrum, various leaves have a good filtering effect on long-wavelength red light, and also a certain filtering effect on short-wavelength blue light, which can effectively help individuals relax — following 李芸, 汝涛涛, 李丝雨 et al., 环境光照对情绪的影响及其作用机制, 心理科学进展, 2022, 30(02): 389–405. Eight leaves were measured in all, each one twice: once under an LED source and once under a bulb.
Detail — Title: Experiment 2 — mood and performance
Detail — Body: Eight testers completed a number game under both lighting conditions: restore eight scrambled numbers to a sequence. Each played three times to get familiar with the game, then played it twice more — the first round under LEDs, the second under light filtered through a plant — answering a NASA-TLX questionnaire after each round, where a lower score is the better result., Overall, the participants’ mood and performance were improved when exposed to the plant-filtered light.
Detail — Title: Making the kit
Detail — Body: The planter shells were printed and the electronics built by hand: LED discs soldered, the copper induction coil wound, strain modules fixed to the leaves, and the whole assembly fitted into the printed box.
Detail — Caption: The kit, apart.
Detail — Items — Caption: Soldering the LED disc.
Detail — Items — Caption: Winding the induction coil.
Detail — Items — Caption: Fixing a module to the leaves.
Detail — Title: What the game leaves behind
Detail — Body: Players can invite others to join collaborative tasks, unlocking hidden features and gradually building a unique plant ecosystem for the community. The game enhances social interaction and fosters a sense of belonging — a delightful way to cultivate neighborly connections and celebrate nature together.
heartwhisper:
Project
Title: HeartWhisper
Summary: A Deep Learning–Based Device for East Asian Family Emotional Communication
Role: Hardware + Deep Learning
Year: 2024
Tags: Product Design, Deep Learning, Hardware
Credits — Category: Product Design, Deep Learning
Credits — Collaborators: Xu Mingxuan, Wang Yuchuan
Credits — Instructor: Ruby Wu
Credits — Contribution: Background Research, Hardware Design, Function Design, Deep Learning, Drawings
Credits — Period: Sep 2024 — Nov 2024
Overview: A device for automated emotional communication that transcends verbal expression — integrating hardware, AI, Arduino, and parametric methods. When verbal communication is inconvenient or strained, HeartWhisper assists family members in expressing their thoughts and emotions: it recognizes emotion in speech in real time, then surfaces both the words and the underlying feelings through printed notes and changes in lighting.
Problem: In East Asian families, parents and children often communicate poorly despite deep love for each other. Communication depends not only on words but on making each other understand emotions — which are very hard to express in such families, especially when both sides are busy or angry.
Approach: Product design integrating hardware, AI, Arduino, and parametric methods. A real-time deep-learning model recognizes emotion from speech; ambient lighting woven through the device expresses the emotional flow detected behind each utterance.
Prototype: Three woven sculptural devices form the family-side fixtures. As family members speak, parents' words and detected emotions are printed onto small paper slips, while LEDs embedded in the woven shells pulse and shift color to express the underlying feelings flowing beneath the speech in real time.
Outcome: The system facilitates ongoing communication during moments of extreme busyness or emotional turbulence — letting family members surface thoughts, feelings, and care for each other when verbal expression feels difficult.
Detail — Text: Mom, using this device, I can feel the emotions whispering beneath the surface of your words.

Detail — Title: The problem
Detail — Body: In East Asian families, many parents and children communicate poorly despite their deep love for one another. Communication depends not only on words but on making each other understand emotions — and emotions are very hard to express in such families, especially when both sides are busy or angry., The findings below come from questionnaire surveys of more than 40 people, social media research, and 20 papers.
Detail — Title: The trauma of intergenerational mobility

Detail — Items — Detail: East Asians often express love subtly or through nonverbal cues, and share good news with family but not bad.

Detail — Intro: Each of the three findings had to turn into something the device actually does.

Detail — Items — Detail: A pair of devices that let you leave a message by speaking one way, with no call to answer and no reply demanded.
Detail — Items — Term: Too busy to call, easy to forget to reply
Detail — Items — Detail: Speech to text, summarised and printed on paper — plus a reminder note when there has been no contact for a long time.
Detail — Items — Term: Emotions expressed inappropriately or misread
Detail — Items — Detail: Deep learning identifies more than one emotion at a time; the two most prominent are visualised as light colours and printed as emoji.
Detail — Title: The device
Detail — Body: A device for automated emotional communication that transcends verbal expression, integrating hardware, AI, Arduino and parametric methods. When communication between family members is inconvenient, or when they are in a cold war, they can use it to help express their thoughts and emotions. It recognises the emotions in speech automatically, and both parties see the thoughts — and the feelings flowing behind them — through printed notes and changes in lighting.
Detail — Title: Four gestures, no screen
Detail — Body: The whole interface is the surface of the shell. There is no display to look at and nothing to unlock, which is the point: the device had to be usable by a parent who would never open an app.

Detail — Items — Detail: Speak your message. The results are conveyed through dynamic lighting and printed notes.

Detail — Items — Term: Shake the device
Detail — Items — Detail: Signals a decline or refusal.
Detail — Items — Term: Inactivity reminder
Detail — Items — Detail: If there is no interaction and the average communication interval is exceeded, the device gently reminds both parties to reconnect.

Detail — Title: Emotion, made visible
Detail — Body: Real-time flowing emotion, flowing light colour. The model picks from the eight emotions judged most suitable in the Mood Wheel — joy, acceptance, worry, surprise, sadness, boredom, anger and concern — and the two most prominent are mixed into the light the shell gives off while the message plays., Aside from the content of speech, other contextual factors also greatly affect emotion detection. By having users enter the relevant information, and detecting the rest from the system, a more accurate emotional output can be achieved.

Detail — Title: Why it looks like a nest
Detail — Body: The form is bionic, taken from bird's nests. A nest is three things at once — something held inside it, a braided layer around that, and a framework carrying the whole thing in the branches. The product is built the same way: circuit board and sensors inside, housings around them, framework holding it up. Pictures of bird's nests plus the functional and ergonomic requirements drove a Grasshopper definition — SubD, random points on the surface, connection, multiple pipe — that generates the braided layer and the framework together.

Detail — Title: Three changes, and why
Detail — Items — Term: The plastic shell became knitted fabric
Detail — Items — Detail: To enhance the warmth of the product and better support communication between parents and children, we replaced the original plastic shell with a unique, lightweight knitted fabric.
Detail — Items — Term: The paper output moved up the body
Detail — Items — Detail: To improve readability, we moved the paper strip output from the bottom to two-thirds of the product's height.

Project
Title: Belt for the Blind
Summary: A Wearable Device Based on Tactile Perception and User Testing
Role: Tactile Perception + Prototype Dev
Year: 2024
Tags: Product Design, Deep Learning, Experimental Design, Prototype Development
Credits — Category: Product Design, Deep Learning, Experimental Design, Prototype Development
Credits — Instructor: Ruby Wu
Credits — Period: Oct 2023 — Oct 2024

Detail — Items — Label: Type
Detail — Items — Value: Product design, deep learning, experimental design, prototype development
Detail — Items — Label: Year
Detail — Items — Value: Oct 2023 — Oct 2024
Detail — Items — Label: Instructor
Detail — Items — Value: Ruby Wu
Detail — Items — Label: Equipment
Detail — Items — Value: Belt-mounted motor module, RF remote control, Li-ion pack, 3D-printed enclosures, Insta360 cameras
Detail — Title: Why not the hands
Detail — Body: The hands were the first part of the body that inspired me: in practice, people often help a blind person by guiding their hands, so that they can sense direction. But freeing the hands to perceive the environment is also crucial for blind individuals — which is the reason the cue had to be carried somewhere else on the body.
Detail — Title: The belt
Detail — Body: What the wearer feels is a motor module carried on a webbing belt at the small of the back. In the trials the motors are driven by a remote operator, and the subject responds to their movement by intuition, having been told nothing about the experiment beforehand.
Detail — Caption: The wearable experimental equipment, laid out and worn.
Detail — Title: Why did I choose the waist?
Detail — Body: Five sites were compared, each with its own MRI cross-section on the board, against one question: where can a symmetrical, tactile cue actually sit on a body that is walking? Head, neck, chest, hands and ankle each answer it badly — for appearance, for suffocation risk, for gender differences in physique, for the hands the blind need free, and for a foot that never holds still.
Detail — Caption: The comparison as the board makes it: five sites, five cross-sections, and the waist answering last.
Detail — Title: The waist
Detail — Body: From the MRI cross-sectional image of the waist, we can observe that the waist has excellent symmetry — the symmetrical shape of the skin’s outer contour, the spine, and the back muscles. This symmetry is crucial for the human body’s sense of direction, ensuring that the perception of left and right is balanced. The large skin surface area at the waist is also highly convenient for wearable devices based on tactile feedback, and using a belt as a carrier makes it easy to integrate electronic components and batteries., The human spine also has a natural indentation at the L5 vertebra, which allows a belt to stay securely in place around the waist. If a navigation wearable device were placed here, it could provide stable directional guidance to the wearer.
Detail — Title: How did I verify the feasibility of the principle?
Detail — Body: In this experiment, I break down the walking path of individuals in the real world into a series of point-to-point segments — a path that can be reconstructed into a complex walking trajectory through integration. The experiment involves a blindfolded subject and a remote operator. The subject must rely on intuition to respond to the movements of the belt motors controlled by the remote operator, and prior to the experiment has no knowledge of the experiment’s details., These are feasibility trials with a blindfolded sighted subject, not tests with blind users.
Detail — Caption: One run, seen from above.
Detail — Caption: The records grid. The whole experiment is recorded by three cameras: an overhead camera that tracks the subject’s walking path, a fixed-position camera that captures the overall process, and a downward-facing motion camera worn on the subject’s back to capture the positional changes of the belt’s motor module — these thirty-two stills are the fixed camera’s.
Detail — Title: Making it
Detail — Body: The belt is webbing, zip ties and printed plastic around a DC gear motor: a driver board and a Li-ion pack in one printed box, the motor in another, and an RF remote so the operator can drive it from across the room.
Detail — Caption: How the belt was made, and what the trial recorded of it: the parts and the build on the left, the module in place and the belt line across the lumbar levels on the right.
